Looking at my land and my situation, I think through what I've been doing for the past 30-odd years. I have about 10 mu of flat, irrigated cropland on the North China Plain. The soil is decent — loamy, a bit saline in patches, but workable.

I don't need to think hard about this. Wheat in winter, maize in summer. That's what everyone in Quzhou does. That's what my father did. The prices are predictable enough, the market is right there in town, and I know exactly how to grow them. At my age, I'm not going to try cotton or something complicated my back can't handle.

For winter wheat, I'll plant my usual improved variety — something from the Jimai line that the local seed shop carries. It does well here and I know how it behaves. I'll rotary till after the maize harvest to bury the stubble, then sow in early October. I'll irrigate three times: the pre-winter water is non-negotiable, then at jointing, then around heading. Water's getting harder to pump and my neighbors say we should cut back, but I'm not going to risk the harvest. I'll put down a full base fertilizer of phosphorus and potassium before seeding, then topdress nitrogen at jointing. Two pesticide passes — one herbicide early on, one fungicide when rust season comes in spring.

For summer maize, right after the wheat harvest in June, I'll direct-seed without tilling. Less work, saves fuel, and the soil is fine enough after rotary the autumn before. Hybrid seed, the same kind I've used for several years. The summer rains usually handle irrigation, but I'll run the pump once if it gets dry around pollination — that's when yield really suffers. One pesticide pass for corn borers if I see them bad.

I'm not going to change what works. Yields around 450 for wheat and 550 for maize are what I expect. That pays the bills and leaves enough for the house.
